question_html: The power of Parliament to levy income-tax (other than agricultural income) is derived from which specific entry of the Constitution of India?

options.A: Entry 82 of List I (Union List) of the Seventh Schedule, read with Article 246
options.B: Entry 82 of List II (State List) of the Seventh Schedule, read with Article 246
options.C: Entry 47 of List III (Concurrent List) of the Seventh Schedule, read with Article 246
options.D: Article 366(28) of the Constitution of India, which independently confers the power to levy income-tax

Entry 82 of the Union List (List I) of the Seventh Schedule to Article 246 of the Constitution empowers Parliament to make laws with respect to taxes on income other than agricultural income. Article 366(28) merely defines 'taxation'; it does not confer taxing power.

options.A: Circulars are binding on both the department and the assessee, whereas Notifications are binding only on the assessee and never on the department
options.B: Circulars and Notifications are, in every respect, legally identical instruments issued by CBDT, differing only in their title

question_html: An Assessing Officer in Chennai (within the jurisdiction of the Madras High Court) is deciding a case where the Madras High Court has ruled one way on a point of law, while the Bombay High Court has ruled the opposite way on an identical point, and the Supreme Court has not yet decided the issue. Which decision must the Assessing Officer necessarily follow?

options.A: The decision of the Bombay High Court, since it was rendered by a High Court with a larger sitting Bench, and larger Benches automatically override smaller ones across all jurisdictions
options.B: Neither decision is binding, as only Supreme Court decisions have any binding force anywhere in India, and non-jurisdictional High Court rulings carry no relevance at all until the Supreme Court rules
options.C: The decision of the Madras High Court, since a High Court's decision is binding on all assessees and authorities within its own jurisdiction, while the Bombay High Court's ruling has only persuasive value in Chennai
options.D: The Assessing Officer may follow whichever decision favours the Revenue, since procedural rules under the Income-tax Act, 2025 permit selecting the interpretation most beneficial to tax collection

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The decision of the Madras High Court, since a High Court's decision is binding on all assessees and authorities within its own jurisdiction, while the Bombay High Court's ruling has only persuasive value in Chennai

A Supreme Court decision is the law of the land and binds all courts/authorities throughout India. A High Court's decision binds all assessees and income-tax authorities within its own jurisdiction; outside its jurisdiction, it has persuasive value only. Here, the Madras High Court decision governs in Chennai.

question_html: As per the charging section (section 4) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, income-tax is a tax leviable on the:

options.A: Total income, of the tax year, of every person, at the rate(s) prescribed by the Annual Finance Act (or the concessional rates under the default tax regime, as applicable), and in the manner laid down under the Act

question_html: Mr. Verma contends that since he is not an Indian citizen, section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 cannot apply to charge tax on his income earned in India. Is this contention correct?

question_html: Which of the following correctly states the key difference between the Mitakshara and Dayabhaga schools of Hindu law in relation to acquisition of a right/share in HUF property?

options.A: Under Dayabhaga law, a child acquires a right/share in family property by birth itself; under Mitakshara law, a right/share arises only upon the death of the head of the family
options.B: Both schools follow identical rules for acquisition of rights by birth, differing only in matters relating to succession upon death
options.C: Under Mitakshara law, a child acquires a right/share in the family property by birth itself, irrespective of whether the head of the family is alive; under Dayabhaga law, no one acquires a right/share by birth, and children acquire a right/share only on the death of the head of the family
options.D: Mitakshara law applies uniformly across the whole of India, while Dayabhaga law applies only to Union Territories and not to any State

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Under Mitakshara law, a child acquires a right/share in the family property by birth itself, irrespective of whether the head of the family is alive; under Dayabhaga law, no one acquires a right/share by birth, and children acquire a right/share only on the death of the head of the family

Under Mitakshara law (prevalent in most of India), a child acquires a right/share in family property by birth, irrespective of whether elders are living. Under Dayabhaga law (prevalent in West Bengal and Assam), no one acquires a right/share by birth as long as the head of the family is alive; children acquire such a right/share only on the father's death.

question_html: ABC Inc., incorporated in the USA, has made prescribed arrangements for declaration and payment of dividends within India out of income chargeable to tax in India. Which of the following is correct?

options.A: ABC Inc. automatically becomes an 'Indian company' under section 2(53) merely by making such arrangements, since 'Indian company' and 'domestic company' are identical, interchangeable terms
options.B: ABC Inc. cannot be treated as a 'domestic company' under any circumstances, since only companies incorporated in India can ever qualify as a 'domestic company'
options.C: ABC Inc. qualifies as a 'domestic company' under section 2(42), even though it is not an 'Indian company' under section 2(53), because 'domestic company' includes any company (Indian or foreign) that has made the prescribed arrangements for declaration and payment of dividends within India
options.D: ABC Inc. remains a 'foreign company' for all purposes, and the making of dividend-declaration arrangements in India has no bearing on its classification under the Act

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) ABC Inc. qualifies as a 'domestic company' under section 2(42), even though it is not an 'Indian company' under section 2(53), because 'domestic company' includes any company (Indian or foreign) that has made the prescribed arrangements for declaration and payment of dividends within India

'Indian company' under section 2(53) means a company formed and registered under the Companies Act (and certain other specified entities). 'Domestic company' under section 2(42) is a wider concept - it means an Indian company OR any other company which, in respect of its income liable to tax in India, has made the prescribed arrangements for declaration and payment of dividends within India.

question_html: A ship belonging to a non-resident carries goods shipped from a port in India. As per section 316, what amount is deemed to be the income of the non-resident chargeable to tax in the SAME tax year in which it is earned, rather than after the year end?

question_html: An assessee receives a cash subsidy from the State Government, which he uses partly to reduce the cost of a depreciable capital asset that he purchases. How is such subsidy treated for the purposes of the definition of 'income' under section 2(49)?

options.A: The entire subsidy is included as 'income' in full, with no carve-out whatsoever, even where a portion is used to reduce the actual cost of a depreciable asset
options.B: The subsidy, grant, cash incentive or similar assistance is generally included as 'income', except to the extent it is taken into account for determining the actual cost of the depreciable asset for depreciation purposes (i.e., the specific portion applied to reduce the actual cost of the asset is carved out from this inclusion, to avoid double benefit/double taxation)
options.C: The entire subsidy is fully exempt from being treated as 'income', regardless of whether or how it is applied by the assessee
options.D: The subsidy is treated as 'income' only if received from the Central Government, and never if received from a State Government

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The subsidy, grant, cash incentive or similar assistance is generally included as 'income', except to the extent it is taken into account for determining the actual cost of the depreciable asset for depreciation purposes (i.e., the specific portion applied to reduce the actual cost of the asset is carved out from this inclusion, to avoid double benefit/double taxation)

Section 2(49) includes subsidies/grants/cash incentives/duty drawbacks/waivers/concessions/reimbursements within 'income', with a specific carve-out for the portion of such assistance taken into account in computing the actual cost of a depreciable asset (since that portion instead reduces the asset's depreciable base rather than being separately taxed as income).

question_html: Under a court decree, Mr. Sharma is required to pay 40% of his professional receipts directly to his former spouse before the receipts even reach him, as a charge on the very source of income itself. Is this amount taxable in the hands of Mr. Sharma?

options.A: Yes, the entire amount is taxable in Mr. Sharma's hands, since any amount paid out of one's own income - whatever the reason - is merely an application of income, which does not reduce taxable income
options.B: No, none of Mr. Sharma's professional receipts are taxable at all, since a court decree of any kind operates to exempt the entire underlying source of income permanently
options.C: No, to the extent this amount represents a genuine diversion of income by overriding title (i.e., the income is diverted at source by virtue of an obligation attached to the source itself, before it reaches Mr. Sharma), it is excluded while computing his taxable income; this is distinguishable from a mere application of income after receipt, which remains taxable
options.D: Yes, but only 50% of the diverted amount is taxable, with the remaining 50% permanently exempt, as a matter of a fixed statutory formula

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No, to the extent this amount represents a genuine diversion of income by overriding title (i.e., the income is diverted at source by virtue of an obligation attached to the source itself, before it reaches Mr. Sharma), it is excluded while computing his taxable income; this is distinguishable from a mere application of income after receipt, which remains taxable

There is a well-recognised distinction between diversion of income by overriding title (where income is diverted before it reaches the assessee, due to an obligation attached to the source - not taxable in the assessee's hands) and mere application of income (where the assessee first receives the income and then applies/spends it for some purpose - remains taxable, since the obligation is only on the income after receipt).

question_html: A manufacturing company sells one of its factory buildings (used for its own manufacturing operations) at a profit, and separately sells finished goods manufactured in the ordinary course of its business. How should the profit from each of these two transactions typically be characterised?

options.A: Both the profit on sale of the factory building and the profit from sale of finished goods are revenue receipts, since both arise from assets owned by the same business entity
options.B: The profit on sale of the factory building represents a realisation of fixed capital and is ordinarily a capital receipt, whereas the profit from sale of finished goods (circulating/trading stock) is a revenue receipt taxable as business income
options.C: Both the profit on sale of the factory building and the profit from sale of finished goods are capital receipts, since both transactions involve a 'sale' in the legal sense
options.D: The profit on sale of the factory building is a revenue receipt because the building was used for business purposes, while the profit from sale of finished goods is a capital receipt since goods are tangible movable property

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The profit on sale of the factory building represents a realisation of fixed capital and is ordinarily a capital receipt, whereas the profit from sale of finished goods (circulating/trading stock) is a revenue receipt taxable as business income

Fixed capital refers to assets acquired and retained for earning profits (e.g., a factory building used in the business) - realisation of such an asset is ordinarily a capital receipt. Circulating capital refers to assets turned over in the course of trade (e.g., stock-in-trade/finished goods) - realisation of such assets is a revenue receipt.

question_html: What is the general test applied to determine whether compensation received for termination of an agency is a capital receipt or a revenue receipt?

options.A: Whether the compensation amount exceeds Rs. 10 lakhs, purely as a fixed monetary threshold, irrespective of the recipient's overall business structure
options.B: Whether the agency agreement was originally reduced to writing, as opposed to being an oral arrangement between the parties
options.C: Whether the termination results in the loss of an agency that forms the very structure of the recipient's entire business (making the compensation a capital receipt), or merely results in the loss of one of several trading agencies/contracts held by the recipient in the ordinary course of business (making the compensation a revenue receipt)
options.D: Whether the principal who terminates the agency is a resident or a non-resident, since only compensation received from a non-resident principal is treated as a capital receipt

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Whether the termination results in the loss of an agency that forms the very structure of the recipient's entire business (making the compensation a capital receipt), or merely results in the loss of one of several trading agencies/contracts held by the recipient in the ordinary course of business (making the compensation a revenue receipt)

The determinative test is the effect of the termination on the recipient's trading structure: loss of a sole agency, forming the entire structure of the business, generally yields a capital receipt; loss of just one of several agencies held in the normal course of a diversified agency business generally yields a revenue receipt.

question_html: A company enters into a contract to purchase specialised machinery (a capital asset) for its factory. The supplier defaults, and the company receives liquidated damages under the contract for the supplier's failure to deliver the machinery. How is this receipt typically characterised?

options.A: As a revenue receipt, since any damages received under a commercial contract are automatically classified as arising in the course of business and therefore as business income

question_html: Where any sum is found credited in the books of a closely-held company and the company offers an explanation about the nature and source of the credit which is treated as being 'share application money, share capital, share premium or any such amount', by whatever name called, what additional requirement applies under section 102, beyond the company's own explanation?

question_html: An assessee is found to have incurred expenditure for which he offers no satisfactory explanation about the source. The amount of such unexplained expenditure is deemed to be his income under section 105. Can the assessee subsequently claim any further deduction in respect of this deemed income?

options.A: No; once an amount is deemed to be income under section 105 on account of unexplained expenditure, no further deduction is allowed in respect of that same deemed income under any other provision of the Act
options.B: Yes, the assessee may claim a deduction equal to 50% of such deemed income as a standard, automatic relief available under section 105 itself

options.D: Yes, but only if the assessee is an individual and not if the assessee is a company or a firm

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No; once an amount is deemed to be income under section 105 on account of unexplained expenditure, no further deduction is allowed in respect of that same deemed income under any other provision of the Act

A specific rule under the unexplained income provisions denies any further deduction in respect of an amount that has already been deemed to be income under section 105 (unexplained expenditure) - the deemed income stands taxed in full, without any offsetting deduction being separately available for the very same amount.

question_html: At what effective rate is income taxed once it is deemed to be unexplained income under any of sections 102 to 106?

options.A: 30%, being a flat rate with no surcharge or cess levied on unexplained income under any circumstances
